claim: TGF-β-associated genes including Nt5e (CD73), Folr4 (folate receptor 4), Foxp3, and Ikzf2 (Helios) are more highly expressed in PSGL1lo Ly6Clo T-betlo CXCR5hi Tfh cells relative to PSGL1hi Ly6Chi T-bethi CXCR5lo Th1 cells during acute LCMV infection.
source: This analysis revealed a number of TGF-β-associated genes commonly found in Treg cells, including Nt5e (CD73), Folr4 (folate receptor 4), Foxp3, and Ikzf2 (Helios) (Hill et al., 2007), to be more highly expressed in PSLG1lo Ly6Clo T-betlo CXCR5hi Tfh cells relative to the PSGL1hi Ly6Chi T-bethi CXCR5lo Th1 cells (Marshall et al., 2011; Hale et al., 2013) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by microarray gene expression data shown in Figure 1A and referenced to prior publications (Marshall et al., 2011; Hale et al., 2013; Hill et al., 2007).

claim: LCMV-specific CD4 T cells do not differentiate into Tfr cells during acute LCMV Armstrong infection.
source: This suggested that LCMV-specific CD4 T cells do not differentiate into Tfr cells (Marshall et al., 2011; Srivastava et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on flow cytometry data showing lack of FoxP3 protein expression and other Treg-associated markers in LCMV-specific CD4 T cells (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), supported by citations.

claim: Tfh cells express enhanced levels of CD73, folate receptor 4, and Helios compared to Th1 cells during LCMV infection.
source: However, in agreement with the differential mRNA expression, we did find enhanced expression of several of the TGF-β- or Treg-associated proteins including CD73, folate receptor 4, and Helios on Tfh cells relative to the Th1 cells (Figure 1C) (Hill et al., 2007; Iyer et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1C and referenced to prior publications (Hill et al., 2007; Iyer et al., 2013).

claim: Direct TGF-β signaling to CD4 T cells promotes the differentiation of Tfh precursor cells at day 3 post LCMV infection.
source: Intriguingly, we found that direct TGF-β promoted the differentiation of Tfh precursor cells at day 3 post infection (p.i.), such that there were about 1/3 fewer CD25lo CXCR5+ Tfh precursor cells in the absence of direct TGF-β signals (WT = 60.25% ± 4, KO = 42% ± 3.3) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from TGF-βRII knockout experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: TGF-βRII KO early effector CD4 T cells express more Th1 proteins Ly6C and T-bet and slightly lower Tfh TF Bcl6 at day 3 post LCMV infection.
source: Additionally, the TGF-βRII KO early effector CD4 T cells expressed more Th1 proteins Ly6C and T-bet and slightly lower Tfh TF Bcl6 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: By day 8 post LCMV infection, there is no phenotypic difference between TGF-βRII WT and KO CD4 T cells in the spleen.
source: However, by day 8 there was no phenotypic difference between TGF-βRII WT and KO CD4 T cells in the spleen (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: Influenza neuraminidase enzyme promotes the cleavage of latent TGF-β complex into its bioactive form in the lung mucosa.
source: Moreover, respiratory influenza infection induces transcription of TGF-β and the influenza neuraminidase enzyme promotes the cleavage of latent TGF-β complex into its bioactive form in the lung mucosa (Schultz-Cherry and Hinshaw, 1996; Carlson et al., 2010; Roberson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior publications (Schultz-Cherry and Hinshaw, 1996; Carlson et al., 2010; Roberson et al., 2012).

claim: The proportion and total number of PSGL1lo Ly6Clo and PD-1hi CXCR5hi Tfh cells in the lung-draining mediastinal lymph node are markedly reduced in the absence of direct TGF-β signals during influenza infection.
source: Moreover, we found that the proportion and total number of PSGL1lo Ly6Clo and PD-1hi CXCR5hi Tfh cells in the lung-draining mediastinal lymph node (MLN) were markedly reduced in the absence of direct TGF-β signals (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from TGF-βRII knockout experiments during influenza infection shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There is an increase in number of PSGL1hi Ly6Chi Th1 cells in all tissues examined in the absence of direct TGF-β signals during influenza infection.
source: Furthermore, there was an increase in number of PSGL1hi Ly6Chi Th1 cells in all tissues examined (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A–C.

claim: TGF-βRII KO influenza-specific CD4 T cells show increased expression of the Th1 TF T-bet and reduced expression of the Tfh TF Bcl6.
source: Concomitant with the cell surface phenotypes, we found increased expression of the Th1 TF T-bet and reduced expression of the Tfh TF Bcl6 as well as increased production of IFN-γ and IL-2 in the TGF-βRII KO influenza-specific CD4 T cells compared to their WT counterparts (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: TGF-βRII KO influenza-specific CD4 T cells show increased production of IFN-γ and IL-2 compared to WT cells.
source: Concomitant with the cell surface phenotypes, we found increased expression of the Th1 TF T-bet and reduced expression of the Tfh TF Bcl6 as well as increased production of IFN-γ and IL-2 in the TGF-βRII KO influenza-specific CD4 T cells compared to their WT counterparts (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by intracellular cytokine staining data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Fewer TGF-βRII KO Stg cells are localized in PNA+ germinal centers in the mediastinal lymph node during influenza infection.
source: Finally, and potentially most importantly given their function to help B cells in the GC, we also detected fewer TGF-βRII KO Stg cells localized in PNA+ GC in the MLN (Figure 2E), suggesting that TGF-β is important for optimal trafficking of Tfh cells to GCs.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescent microscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Direct TGF-β signaling is important for the generation of Tfh cells while it suppresses Th1 differentiation during respiratory influenza virus infection.
source: Together, these data suggest that direct TGF-β signaling was important for the generation of Tfh cells, while it suppressed Th1 differentiation during respiratory influenza virus infection.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing reduced Tfh and increased Th1 cells in TGF-βRII KO conditions (Figures 2A-E).

claim: Adoptive transfer of WT CD4 T cells largely restores the number of Fas+ GL7+ GC B cells and IgMlo B cells in OT-II recipient mice infected with influenza.
source: Importantly, we found that the adoptive transfer of WT CD4 T cells largely restored B cell help in the OT-II recipient mice such that there was an enhanced number Fas+ GL7+ GC B cells and IgMlo B cells in the MLN 14 days p.i.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from adoptive transfer experiments (Figure 4A).

claim: TGF-βRII KO CD4 T cells are unable to rescue the formation of GC B cells in OT-II recipient mice during influenza infection.
source: However, the TGF-βRII KO CD4 T cells were unable to rescue the formation of GC B cells in these chimeric mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: WT CD4 T cells partially rescue GC B cell class switching to the IgG1 subtype, while TGF-βRII KO CD4 T cells do so less efficiently, particularly in the spleen.
source: Further, WT CD4 T cells partially rescued GC B cell class switching to the IgG1 subtype, while the TGF-βRII KO CD4 T cells did so less efficiently, particularly in the spleen (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mice receiving TGF-βRII KO CD4 T cells have fewer and smaller germinal centers in the spleen compared to those receiving WT CD4 T cells during influenza infection.
source: In addition to the enumeration of GC B cells by flow cytometry, we also observed fewer and smaller GCs from the spleens of mice receiving TGF-βRII KO CD4 T cells by fluorescent microscopy (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescent microscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: T cell-directed TGF-β is important for influenza-specific IgG and IgA in the airways of infected mice.
source: Finally, T cell-directed TGF-β was also important for influenza-specific IgG and IgA in the airways of infected mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data from bronchoalveolar lavage fluid shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Intrinsic TGF-β signaling in antiviral T cells is required for Tfh cell function as B cell helpers, GC reactions, and isotype-switched antibody responses during respiratory influenza virus infection.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate a previously unappreciated requirement of intrinsic TGF-β signaling in antiviral T cells for Tfh cell function as B cell helpers, and thus, GC reactions and isotype-switched antibody responses during respiratory influenza virus infection.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing defects in GC B cells and antibody responses in TGF-βRII KO conditions (Figure 4).

claim: TGF-βRII KO CD4 T cells display enhanced Th1 attributes including enhanced expression of CD25, Ly6C, T-bet, IFN-γ, and IL-2 at days 4-5 post influenza infection.
source: Although a difference in Bcl6 expression in the TGF-βRII KO CD4 T cells was not observed at this time point, the TGF-βRII KO CD4 T cells displayed enhanced Th1 attributes including enhanced expression of CD25, Ly6C, T-bet, IFN-γ, and IL-2 (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Direct TGF-β suppresses Th1 precursor formation within the first few days of influenza virus infection.
source: These findings suggested that direct TGF-β suppressed Th1 precursor formation within the first few days of influenza virus infection.
evidence: Inferred from data showing enhanced Th1 markers in TGF-βRII KO cells at days 4-5 post infection (Figure 5).

claim: Addition of recombinant TGF-β (10 ng/ml) to Stg CD4 T cell cultures stimulated with GP66 peptide in vitro does not inhibit T cell activation.
source: Addition of recombinant TGF-β (10 ng/ml) to Stg CD4 T cell cultures stimulated with GP66 peptide in vitro did not inhibit T cell activation because the upregulation of CD25 and the proliferation rates of the CD4 T cells were comparable between cultures containing or lacking exogenous TGF-β (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by in vitro culture data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: TGF-β profoundly affects the ability of activated CD4 T cells to sustain CD25 expression and IL-2 responsiveness in vitro.
source: However, TGF-β profoundly affected the ability of the activated CD4 T cells to sustain CD25 expression and IL-2 responsiveness. That is, at day 2 post activation, the amount of surface CD25 and intracellular phospho-STAT5 (pSTAT5) after IL-2 stimulation was the same whether or not TGF-β was present, but 1 day later, the T cells exposed to TGF-β displayed considerably less CD25 and lower IL-2 responsiveness compared with those that were not (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by in vitro culture data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: TGF-βRII KO early effector cells show a considerably enhanced CD25+ pSTAT5+ population relative to WT cells at day 3 post LCMV infection in vivo.
source: We observed a considerably enhanced CD25+ pSTAT5+ population from TGF-βRII KO early effector cells relative to the WT cells (Figure 6B), suggestive of heightened IL-2 signaling in the TGF-βRII KO CD4 T cells in vivo during infection.
evidence: Supported by ex vivo phospho-flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: TGF-βRII KO early effector cells show enhanced ex vivo CD25+ pS6+ populations at day 3 post LCMV infection, indicating amplified STAT5 and AKT/mTOR signaling.
source: Further, we also found enhanced ex vivo CD25+ pS6+ early effector cells (Figure 6B), indicating that both STAT5 and AKT/mTOR signaling arms are amplified in the absence of TGF-β signals.
evidence: Supported by ex vivo phospho-flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: TGF-β directly suppresses the expression of CD25 and phosphorylation of STAT5 and S6 in early effector CD4 T cells in vivo during infection.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that TGF-β directly suppresses the expression of CD25 and phosphorylation of STAT5 and S6 in early effector CD4 T cells in vivo and thus, likely promotes Tfh cell differentiation by limiting IL-2 signaling in Tfh precursor cells.
evidence: Inferred from ex vivo phospho-flow data showing enhanced CD25, pSTAT5, and pS6 in TGF-βRII KO cells (Figure 6B).

claim: Rapamycin treatment rescues the differentiation of PSGL1lo Ly6Clo Tfh cells in the absence of TGF-βRII signaling during influenza infection.
source: Interestingly, we found that rapamycin treatment rescued the differentiation of PSGL1lo Ly6Clo Tfh cells and suppressed the aberrant expansion of the PSGL1hi Ly6Chi Th1 cells that arise in the absence of direct TGF-β signals (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from rapamycin treatment experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Rapamycin treatment suppresses the aberrant expansion of PSGL1hi Ly6Chi Th1 cells that arise in the absence of direct TGF-β signals during influenza infection.
source: Interestingly, we found that rapamycin treatment rescued the differentiation of PSGL1lo Ly6Clo Tfh cells and suppressed the aberrant expansion of the PSGL1hi Ly6Chi Th1 cells that arise in the absence of direct TGF-β signals (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from rapamycin treatment experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Rapamycin suppresses the over-expression of T-bet and GrzB in TGF-βRII KO CD4 T cells during influenza infection.
source: Likewise, rapamycin suppressed the over-expression of T-bet and GrzB in the TGF-βRII KO CD4 T cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: TGF-β dampens mTOR activity in CD4 T cells to allow for Tfh cell differentiation.
source: Taking into account that mTOR blockade with rapamycin affects many other cell types, these results suggest that TGF-β dampens mTOR activity in CD4 T cells to allow for Tfh cell differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from rapamycin rescue experiments showing restoration of Tfh differentiation in TGF-βRII KO cells (Figure 6C-D).

claim: T cell-directed TGF-β signals are critical for insulating early effector CD4 T cells from Th1-promoting IL-2 signals, thereby allowing for virus-specific Tfh cell differentiation.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that T cell-directed TGF-β signals are critical for insulating early effector CD4 T cells from Th1-promoting IL-2 signals, thereby allowing for virus-specific Tfh cell differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing TGF-β suppression of CD25, IL-2 signaling, and promotion of Tfh differentiation.

claim: T cell intrinsic TGF-βRII signaling is required for GC reactions and isotype-switched antibody production during respiratory influenza virus infection.
source: Consequently, T cell intrinsic TGF-βRII signaling is also required for GC reactions and isotype-switched antibody production during respiratory influenza virus infection.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing defects in GC B cells and antibody responses in TGF-βRII KO conditions (Figure 4).

claim: TGF-β was recently shown in human T cells to promote the differentiation of certain Tfh properties in vitro.
source: In support of these findings, TGF-β was also recently shown in human T cells to promote the differentiation of certain Tfh properties in vitro (Schmitt et al., 2014b).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior publication (Schmitt et al., 2014b).

claim: T cell-directed TGF-β restricts the expression of the high affinity IL-2Rα chain CD25 on early effector CD4 T cells in vitro and in vivo.
source: T cell-directed TGF-β restricted the expression of the high affinity IL-2Rα chain CD25 on early effector CD4 T cells in vitro and in vivo, while, early anti-viral effector cells generated in the absence of TGF-β signals displayed evidence of enhanced IL-2 signaling in vivo.
evidence: Supported by in vitro culture data (Figure 6A) and ex vivo phospho-flow data (Figure 6B).

claim: Early anti-viral effector cells generated in the absence of TGF-β signals display evidence of enhanced IL-2 signaling in vivo.
source: T cell-directed TGF-β restricted the expression of the high affinity IL-2Rα chain CD25 on early effector CD4 T cells in vitro and in vivo, while, early anti-viral effector cells generated in the absence of TGF-β signals displayed evidence of enhanced IL-2 signaling in vivo.
evidence: Supported by ex vivo phospho-flow data showing enhanced pSTAT5 in TGF-βRII KO cells (Figure 6B).

claim: IL-2 promotes Blimp1 expression and Th1 differentiation.
source: Since IL-2 promotes Blimp1 expression and Th1 differentiation (Pepper et al., 2011; Ballesteros-Tato et al., 2012; Johnston et al., 2012; Nurieva et al., 2012; Oestreich et al., 2012), these data suggest that TGF-β works to insulate early effector CD4 T cells from IL-2 signals and may play a central role in limiting Blimp1 expression in Tfh progenitor cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior publications (Pepper et al., 2011; Ballesteros-Tato et al., 2012; Johnston et al., 2012; Nurieva et al., 2012; Oestreich et al., 2012).

claim: TGF-β works to insulate early effector CD4 T cells from IL-2 signals and may play a central role in limiting Blimp1 expression in Tfh progenitor cells.
source: Since IL-2 promotes Blimp1 expression and Th1 differentiation (Pepper et al., 2011; Ballesteros-Tato et al., 2012; Johnston et al., 2012; Nurieva et al., 2012; Oestreich et al., 2012), these data suggest that TGF-β works to insulate early effector CD4 T cells from IL-2 signals and may play a central role in limiting Blimp1 expression in Tfh progenitor cells.
evidence: Inferred from data showing TGF-β suppression of CD25 and IL-2 signaling, combined with knowledge that IL-2 promotes Blimp1.

claim: TGF-β signaling in B cells promotes IgA class switching and mucosal immunity.
source: Interestingly, TGF-β signaling in B cells also promotes IgA class switching and mucosal immunity (Cazac and Roes, 2000; Borsutzky et al., 2004; Seo et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior publications (Cazac and Roes, 2000; Borsutzky et al., 2004; Seo et al., 2013).

claim: TGF-β is important for the differentiation of both mucosal Tfh and B cells, which must interact for proper antibody responses.
source: Since TGF-β is important for the differentiation of both mucosal Tfh and B cells, which also must interact for proper antibody responses, this provides a unique example of a coordinated signaling pathway to maximize humoral immunity to respiratory influenza virus infection.
evidence: Inferred from current study findings on Tfh cells and cited prior work on B cells.

claim: Cytokines utilizing the STAT3 signaling pathway including IL-6, IL-21, and IL-27 have been implicated in driving Tfh differentiation.
source: Cytokines utilizing the STAT3 signaling pathway including IL-6, IL-21, and IL-27 have been implicated in driving Tfh differentiation (Nurieva et al., 2008; Batten et al., 2010; Eto et al., 2011; Ma et al., 2012; Choi et al., 2013a; Harker et al., 2013; Ray et al., 2014), but due to their partially compensatory pathways, separating the requirements for individual signals throughout infection has proved challenging.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior publications (Nurieva et al., 2008; Batten et al., 2010; Eto et al., 2011; Ma et al., 2012; Choi et al., 2013a; Harker et al., 2013; Ray et al., 2014).

claim: TGF-β is an additional signal that may restrict IL-2-induced Blimp1 and directly suppress T-bet expression to allow for Tfh cell differentiation.
source: Herein, we identify TGF-β as an additional signal that may restrict IL-2-induced Blimp1 and directly suppress T-bet expression to allow for Tfh cell differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing TGF-β suppression of IL-2 signaling and Th1 markers.

claim: A subset of human Tfh cells share multiple properties with Th17 cells including co-expression of Bcl6 and Rorγt and the ability to provide B cell help.
source: In fact, a subset of human Tfh cells share multiple properties with that of Th17 cells including co-expression of Bcl6 and Rorγt and the ability to provide B cell help (Schmitt et al., 2014a, 2014b).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior publications (Schmitt et al., 2014a, 2014b).

claim: Rorγt expression was not detected in murine anti-viral effector CD4 T cells.
source: However, we did not detect Rorγt expression in murine anti-viral effector CD4 T cells (data not shown).
evidence: Based on experimental observation (data not shown).

claim: Addition of TGF-β to murine T cell cultures in the presence of IL-6 and IL-21 induces IL-17-producing T cells but suppresses Tfh properties including ICOS and IL-21 expression.
source: Moreover, addition of TGF-β to murine T cell cultures in the presence of IL-6 and IL-21 induced IL-17-producing T cells as expected, but actually suppressed Tfh properties including ICOS and IL-21 expression (Schmitt et al., 2014b).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior publication (Schmitt et al., 2014b).

claim: TGF-β and STAT3 signals are required for murine Tfh differentiation during viral infection in vivo, but are not sufficient to induce this cell fate in vitro.
source: These data suggest that although TGF-β and STAT3 signals are required for murine Tfh differentiation during viral infection in vivo, they are not sufficient to induce this cell fate in vitro and that the specification of Tfh cells by these factors is under tight regulation in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from in vivo and in vitro experimental observations.

claim: IL-12-STAT4 signaling may be required to induce a low level of T-bet in murine Tfh precursor cells to prevent Th17 development.
source: Since STAT4 signaling via IL-12 can promote early Tfh properties including Bcl6 expression (Nakayamada et al., 2011), it is possible that IL-12-STAT4 signaling is also required to induce a low level of T-bet in murine Tfh precursor cells to prevent Th17 development, but this will have to be formally evaluated.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on prior publication (Nakayamada et al., 2011).

claim: Blocking mTOR with rapamycin during the first week of influenza infection is sufficient to restore Tfh cell differentiation and suppress T-bet and GrzB expression in the absence of TGF-β.
source: In the absence of TGF-β, blocking mTOR with rapamycin during the first week of infection was sufficient to restore Tfh cell differentiation and suppress T-bet and GrzB expression.
evidence: Supported by rapamycin treatment experiments (Figure 6C-D).

claim: Rapamycin treatment has no overt effect on the differentiation of WT Stg cells during the first week of influenza infection.
source: However, rapamycin treatment had no overt affect on the differentiation of WT Stg cells during this phase of influenza infection.
evidence: Based on experimental observation from rapamycin treatment experiments.

claim: Rapamycin promotes heterosubtypic immunity to influenza by reducing GC reactions and switched antibody responses, resulting in enhanced levels of protective influenza-specific IgM antibodies.
source: Interestingly, rapamycin was recently reported to promote heterosubtypic immunity to influenza by reducing GC reactions and switched antibody responses, resulting in enhanced levels of protective influenza-specific IgM antibodies (Keating et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior publication (Keating et al., 2013).

claim: The protective effects of rapamycin on heterosubtypic immunity depend on both CD4 T and B cells, with B cell-intrinsic mTORC1 activity responsible for enhancing Aicda expression and class switching.
source: This study showed that the protective effects of rapamycin depended on both CD4 T and B cells, and that B cell-intrinsic mTORC1 activity was responsible for enhancing Aicda expression and class switching.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior publication (Keating et al., 2013).

claim: Suppression of mTOR in virus-specific CD4 T cells would likely suppress Th1 in favor of Tfh cell differentiation, possibly contributing to the protective effects of rapamycin on heterosubtypic immunity to influenza.
source: Although the generation of Tfh cells was not examined in this prior study, our new findings would suggest that suppression of mTOR in the virus-specific CD4 T cells would likely suppress Th1 in favor of Tfh cell differentiation, possibly contributing to the protective effects of rapamycin on heterosubtypic immunity to influenza.
evidence: Inferred from current study findings combined with prior publication (Keating et al., 2013).

claim: Treg cells are required for Tfh differentiation and GC reactions during influenza infection.
source: In support of this hypothesis, Treg cells were recently shown to be required for Tfh differentiation and GC reactions during influenza infection (Leon et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior publication (Leon et al., 2014).

claim: Treg cells appear to play a central role in effector CD4 T cell fates during viral infection, likely by controlling the local bioavailability of both IL-2 and TGF-β.
source: Thus, Treg cells appear to play a central role in effector CD4 T cell fates during viral infection, likely by controlling the local bioavailability of both IL-2 and TGF-β.
evidence: Inferred from current study findings and prior publication on Treg cells (Leon et al., 2014).

claim: Influenza-specific pTreg cells can temper pulmonary inflammation upon secondary or heterologous infections.
source: Another potential consideration is the differentiation of influenza-specific pTreg cells, which can temper pulmonary inflammation upon secondary or heterologous infections (Brincks et al., 2013; Kraft et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior publications (Brincks et al., 2013; Kraft et al., 2013).

claim: IL-2 initiates a dominant positive feedback loop involving IL-2, STAT5, Blimp1, and FoxP3 to maintain the full Treg program in pTreg cells.
source: It is likely that IL-2 itself is playing an important role in this setting by initiating a dominant positive feedback loop involving IL-2, STAT5, Blimp1, and FoxP3 to maintain the full Treg program in pTreg cells (de la Rosa et al., 2004; Fontenot et al., 2005) and that TGF-β may only be required for the initial induction of FoxP3, but this remains to be addressed.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on prior publications (de la Rosa et al., 2004; Fontenot et al., 2005).

claim: TGF-β plays a critical role in mucosal tissues in the formation of tissue-resident memory CD8 T cells.
source: Since TGF-β plays a critical role in mucosal tissues in the formation of tissue-resident memory CD8 T cells (Mackay et al., 2013; Zhang and Bevan, 2013), IgA-producing B cells (Cazac and Roes, 2000; Borsutzky et al., 2004), and as revealed here Tfh cells, it is an attractive target to consider in the development of a broadly protective universal influenza vaccine.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior publications (Mackay et al., 2013; Zhang and Bevan, 2013).

claim: TGF-β is an attractive target to consider in the development of a broadly protective universal influenza vaccine.
source: Since TGF-β plays a critical role in mucosal tissues in the formation of tissue-resident memory CD8 T cells (Mackay et al., 2013; Zhang and Bevan, 2013), IgA-producing B cells (Cazac and Roes, 2000; Borsutzky et al., 2004), and as revealed here Tfh cells, it is an attractive target to consider in the development of a broadly protective universal influenza vaccine.
evidence: Inferred from current study findings and prior publications on TGF-β roles in mucosal immunity.

claim: During acute viral infections, CD4 T cells differentiate into primarily T helper 1 (Th1) and T follicular helper (Tfh) effector cells.
source: During acute viral infections, CD4 T cells differentiate into primarily T helper 1 (Th1) and T follicular helper (Tfh) effector cells (Marshall et al., 2011; Johnston et al., 2012; Hale et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior publications (Marshall et al., 2011; Johnston et al., 2012; Hale et al., 2013).

claim: Th1 cells express the transcription factors T-bet and Blimp1, the effector molecules IFN-γ, TNFα, and in many cases granzyme B and perforin.
source: Similar to CD8 T cells, Th1 cells express the transcription factors (TF) T-bet and Blimp1, the effector molecules IFN-γ, TNFα, (and in many cases granzyme B [GrzB] and perforin) and migrate to sites of viral replication to eliminate infected cells.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about Th1 cells.

claim: Tfh cells primarily remain in secondary lymphoid tissues where they communicate with B cells in germinal centers to facilitate antibody affinity maturation and isotype switching.
source: In contrast, Tfh cells primarily remain in secondary lymphoid tissues where they communicate with B cells in germinal centers (GC) to facilitate antibody affinity maturation and isotype switching.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about Tfh cell function.

claim: Tfh cells express substantially lower levels of T-bet, and instead of Blimp1 they express the TF Bcl6.
source: Tfh cells express substantially lower levels of T-bet, and instead of Blimp1 they express the TF Bcl6.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about Tfh cell markers.

claim: Pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-12, IFN-γ, IFN-αβ, and IL-2 promote Th1 differentiation.
source: Some pro-inflammatory cytokines induced during infection, such as IL-12, IFN-γ, IFN-αβ, and IL-2, promote Th1 differentiation; however, the signals required for Tfh differentiation during viral infection have not been as well characterized.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about Th1 differentiation signals.

claim: Tfh precursor cells start to express the TF Bcl6 and the chemokine receptor CXCR5 as they downregulate CCR7 and PSGL1 following activation.
source: Following activation, Tfh precursor cells start to express the TF Bcl6 and the chemokine receptor CXCR5, as they downregulate CCR7 and P-selectin glycoprotein ligand 1 (PSGL1) (Johnston et al., 2009; Poholek et al., 2010; Choi et al., 2011; Pepper et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior publications (Johnston et al., 2009; Poholek et al., 2010; Choi et al., 2011; Pepper et al., 2011).

claim: Tfh precursor cells migrate toward the interfollicular zone and T-B border where they meet peptide-MHC and costimulatory ligands such as ICOSL from B cells.
source: These events allow for the migration of activated Tfh precursor cells toward the interfollicular zone and T-B border where they again meet peptide-MHC as well as other costimulatory ligands such as Inducible T cell Costimulator ligand (ICOSL) from B cells (Breitfeld et al., 2000; Schaerli et al., 2000; Hardtke et al., 2005; Kerfoot et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior publications (Breitfeld et al., 2000; Schaerli et al., 2000; Hardtke et al., 2005; Kerfoot et al., 2011).

claim: Interactions between Tfh precursor cells and B cells result in further upregulation of Bcl6, migration into the GC, and ability to assist B cells in affinity maturation and proper isotype switching.
source: These interactions result in the further upregulation of Bcl6, migration into the GC, and ability to assist B cells in affinity maturation and proper isotype switching (Poholek et al., 2010; Baumjohann et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior publications (Poholek et al., 2010; Baumjohann et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2011).

claim: IL-6 appears to act on early anti-viral Tfh precursors.
source: For example, IL-6 appears to act on early anti-viral Tfh precursors (Choi et al., 2013a), and while it is not absolutely required for fully differentiated Tfh effector cells during acute lymphocytic choriomeningitis (LCMV) infection (Poholek et al., 2010; Eto et al., 2011), it does promote the sustained activation of Tfh cells during chronic LCMV infection (Harker et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior publications (Choi et al., 2013a; Poholek et al., 2010; Eto et al., 2011; Harker et al., 2011).

claim: IL-6 is not absolutely required for fully differentiated Tfh effector cells during acute LCMV infection.
source: For example, IL-6 appears to act on early anti-viral Tfh precursors (Choi et al., 2013a), and while it is not absolutely required for fully differentiated Tfh effector cells during acute lymphocytic choriomeningitis (LCMV) infection (Poholek et al., 2010; Eto et al., 2011), it does promote the sustained activation of Tfh cells during chronic LCMV infection (Harker et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior publications (Poholek et al., 2010; Eto et al., 2011).

claim: IL-6 promotes the sustained activation of Tfh cells during chronic LCMV infection.

evidence: Supported by citation to prior publication (Harker et al., 2011).

claim: IL-27 is required for Tfh differentiation during protein immunization.

evidence: Supported by citation to prior publication (Batten et al., 2010).

evidence: Supported by citations to prior publications (Nurieva et al., 2008; Vogelzang et al., 2008; Eto et al., 2011; Karnowski et al., 2012).

claim: STAT4 signaling via IL-12 may promote early Tfh progenitor cells during infection.
source: In addition to STAT3, STAT4 signaling via IL-12 may also promote early Tfh progenitor cells during infection (Nakayamada et al., 2011) and appears to be critical for the differentiation of human Tfh cells (Schmitt et al., 2009, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior publication (Nakayamada et al., 2011).

claim: STAT4 signaling appears to be critical for the differentiation of human Tfh cells.
source: In addition to STAT3, STAT4 signaling via IL-12 may also promote early Tfh progenitor cells during infection (Nakayamada et al., 2011) and appears to be critical for the differentiation of human Tfh cells (Schmitt et al., 2009, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior publications (Schmitt et al., 2009, 2013).

claim: STAT4 signals are absolutely required for the differentiation of Th1 cells.
source: However, STAT4 signals are absolutely required for the differentiation of Th1 cells, suggesting that additional signals are needed to repress the expression of the Th1 TFs T-bet and Blimp1 in Tfh progenitor cells.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about STAT4 and Th1 differentiation.

claim: Increased expression of the high affinity IL-2Rα chain CD25 on early effector CD4 T cells correlates with enhanced expression of the Th1 TFs T-bet and Blimp1 and lower levels of the Tfh TF Bcl6.
source: Increased expression of the high affinity IL-2Rα chain CD25 on early effector CD4 T cells correlates with enhanced expression of the Th1 TFs T-bet and Blimp1 and lower levels of the Tfh TF Bcl6 and this is driven largely by IL-2-STAT5 signaling (Choi et al., 2011; Pepper et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2013b).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior publications (Choi et al., 2011; Pepper et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2013b).

claim: CD25lo early effectors have greater potential to generate Tfh cells.
source: In contrast, CD25lo early effectors have greater potential to generate Tfh cells (Ballesteros-Tato et al., 2012; Johnston et al., 2012; Nurieva et al., 2012; Choi et al., 2013b).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior publications (Ballesteros-Tato et al., 2012; Johnston et al., 2012; Nurieva et al., 2012; Choi et al., 2013b).

claim: IL-2 signals are important for the homeostasis of regulatory T cells.
source: Intriguingly, IL-2 signals are also important for the homeostasis of regulatory T cells (Treg).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about IL-2 and Treg cells.

claim: TGF-β promotes the differentiation of peripherally derived regulatory T cells (pTreg) and inhibits the development of autoreactive T cell responses.
source: As an immune-suppressive factor, TGF-β promotes the differentiation of peripherally derived regulatory T cells (pTreg) and inhibits the development of autoreactive T cell responses.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about TGF-β and Treg cells.

claim: TGF-β can serve a pro-inflammatory role by inducing the differentiation of effector Th17 cells.
source: In contrast, TGF-β can also serve a pro-inflammatory role by inducing the differentiation of effector Th17 cells.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about TGF-β and Th17 cells.

claim: T cell-specific ablation of TGF-β signaling demonstrates that direct TGF-β signals are important for both Treg homeostasis and suppression of effector T cell activation and proliferation.
source: T cell-specific ablation of TGF-β signaling, either via TGF-βRII deletion or expression of a dominant negative receptor, has demonstrated that direct TGF-β signals are important for both Treg homeostasis and suppression of effector T cell activation and proliferation (Li et al., 2006; Marie et al., 2006; Sanjabi et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior publications (Li et al., 2006; Marie et al., 2006; Sanjabi et al., 2009).

claim: The aberrant activation of effector cells in the absence of TGF-β signals cannot be rescued by addition of Treg.
source: The aberrant activation of effector cells in the absence of TGF-β signals cannot be rescued by addition of Treg (Li et al., 2006), indicating that direct TGF-β signaling on effector CD4 T cells is required to maintain their homeostasis.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior publication (Li et al., 2006).

claim: Direct TGF-β signaling on effector CD4 T cells is required to maintain their homeostasis.
source: The aberrant activation of effector cells in the absence of TGF-β signals cannot be rescued by addition of Treg (Li et al., 2006), indicating that direct TGF-β signaling on effector CD4 T cells is required to maintain their homeostasis.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results cited in prior publication (Li et al., 2006).

claim: TGF-β suppresses T-bet expression.

evidence: Supported by citations to prior publications (Gorelik et al., 2002; Park et al., 2005).

claim: T cells that proliferate exuberantly in the absence of TGF-β display Th1 attributes.
source: Furthermore, TGF-β suppresses T-bet expression (Gorelik et al., 2002; Park et al., 2005) and the exuberant proliferation of T cells display Th1 attributes (Ishigame et al., 2013), demonstrating that TGF-β has the capacity to suppress Th1 differentiation.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior publication (Ishigame et al., 2013).

claim: TGF-β has the capacity to suppress Th1 differentiation.

evidence: Inferred from cited evidence showing TGF-β suppression of T-bet and Th1 attributes (Gorelik et al., 2002; Park et al., 2005; Ishigame et al., 2013).

claim: Direct TGF-β signaling to CD4 T cells is important for the formation of influenza-specific Tfh cells, GC reactions, and development of isotype-switched, flu-specific antibody responses.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that direct TGF-β signaling to CD4 T cells is important for the formation of influenza-specific Tfh cells, GC reactions, and development of isotype-switched, flu-specific antibody responses.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental results throughout the manuscript (Figures 2-4).

claim: Early during infection, TGF-β signaling suppresses the expression of CD25 on virus-specific CD4 T cells.
source: Early during infection, TGF-β signaling suppressed the expression of the high affinity IL-2 receptor α chain (CD25) on virus-specific CD4 T cells, which tempered IL-2 signaling and STAT5 and mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) activation in Tfh precursor CD4 T cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figures 5, 6A-B).

claim: TGF-β signaling tempers IL-2 signaling and STAT5 and mTOR activation in Tfh precursor CD4 T cells.
source: Early during infection, TGF-β signaling suppressed the expression of the high affinity IL-2 receptor α chain (CD25) on virus-specific CD4 T cells, which tempered IL-2 signaling and STAT5 and mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) activation in Tfh precursor CD4 T cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced pSTAT5 and pS6 with TGF-β (Figure 6A-B).

claim: Inhibition of mTOR allows for the differentiation of Tfh cells in the absence of TGF-βR signaling.
source: Inhibition of mTOR allowed for the differentiation of Tfh cells in the absence of TGF-βR signaling, suggesting that TGF-β insulates Tfh progenitor cells from IL-2-delivered mTOR signals, thereby promoting Tfh differentiation during acute viral infection.
evidence: Supported by rapamycin rescue experiments (Figure 6C-D).

claim: TGF-β insulates Tfh progenitor cells from IL-2-delivered mTOR signals, thereby promoting Tfh differentiation during acute viral infection.
source: Inhibition of mTOR allowed for the differentiation of Tfh cells in the absence of TGF-βR signaling, suggesting that TGF-β insulates Tfh progenitor cells from IL-2-delivered mTOR signals, thereby promoting Tfh differentiation during acute viral infection.
evidence: Inferred from rapamycin rescue experiments and data showing TGF-β suppression of IL-2 signaling (Figure 6).
